pr.title: Have find exit as grep does, and correct a refused-address row
pr.head: f9d922cce4f410b3f99c9f62bf35e12dbf82189d

summary: multipass is a command-line password manager. Its websites plan, which is ready but not built yet, adds a website field to each entry and a multipass find <url> command that prints the names of the entries for a web page, so a browser extension or the Mac app can offer the right login on the right site.

A script that calls find needs to know whether the page simply has no entry or whether something went wrong, such as a wrong passphrase. multipass exits with status 1 on every error today, so if find also exited 1 for "no match", the script would have to read the error text to tell the two apart. The plan left that choice to the owner.
This pull request records the owner's answer: find exits as grep does. It changes only the plan document.

StatusMeaning
0At least one entry matches.
1No entry matches. Related entries, if any, are named on stderr.
2An error, such as a refused page address, a wrong passphrase, or a store that cannot be read.
While moving the acceptance rows for refused addresses to status 2, the author also fixed one row that contradicted the plan's own parsing rules, as the group below explains.

cards.title: Where the review stands
cards.html:
• One open finding: the plan says every other command keeps exiting 1 on any error, but multipass upgrade already exits with 65, 69, or the installer's own status.
  • Four suggestions: say that status 2 covers every error, a usage error and a declined Touch ID sheet included; name the statuses in the plan's changes-by-file rows for src/main.rs and README.md; add an acceptance row for a wrong passphrase; and extend the look-alike address test to the corrected case.
  • One follow-up: the plan does not say how find opens the store while a Touch ID session is unlocked.

cards.title: Terms
cards.html:
• Exit status: the number a command returns to the shell, which a script tests with if or $?.
  • Authority: the part of a web address between :// and the first /, ?, or #; it holds the host and port.
  • Refused address: a page address the plan's strict parser rejects because a browser would read its host differently.
  • Session unlock: the background agent that keeps the store open between commands and asks for a touch of Touch ID instead of the passphrase.

groups.title: The websites plan
groups.kicker: How find reports its result, and one corrected acceptance row
intro: Three parts of the plan change. § 2.2, which describes matching, gains the table of exit statuses and a sentence saying every other command is unchanged. § 6, the plan's decided questions, records the choice and the alternative the owner rejected: status 1 for every failure. § 4, the acceptance criteria, moves its rows for refused addresses from "fails" to "exits 2".

The corrected row concerns the address https://evil.example\@github.com/. The plan refuses an address that holds an @ in its authority, because a browser reads the text before the @ as a user name and password. It runs that check before every other rule and never repeats such an address in an error, since the text before the @ may be a real password. The old row expected an error naming the address because of its backslash, which broke that rule. The row now expects the @ error without the address, and a new row covers a backslash on its own, which may be named.

files.note: The plan for the website field and find: § 2.2 gains the exit-status table, § 4 its refused-address rows, and § 6 the decision.

checks.text: Open finding: "Every other command keeps exiting 1 on any error" is not true today. multipass upgrade exits with 65 or 69 when it fails, or with the installer's own status, as run_upgrade in src/main.rs shows. § 6 item 2 repeats the claim.

§ 2.2: status 2 lists three errors. A declined Touch ID sheet (the request was not approved) and a mistyped command are errors too, and main turns every error into status 1 today, so the implementation has to route find's errors to 2 on purpose.

§ 4: checked against § 2.1. The authority of https://evil.example\@github.com/ runs to the first /, so it holds the @, the @ check runs first, and its error must not name the address. The new row on line 150 holds no @, so naming it is allowed.
